visit.ground: 160 acres outside Castletown in Laois, bordered by the railway line. Good tillage ground at the top of the farm, running down into wet, peaty bog land at the back. About a third tillage, a third silage and a third grazing.

film_intro: Filmed by Provenance on the farm.
story: Rathphelan Farm is 160 acres outside Castletown in Laois. It was originally bought by Liam's great grandmother in the early 1900s and has been farmed by every generation since. Liam now runs the farm with help from his father, who taught him everything, and his wife takes care of the beef boxes and the website. In his words, he makes the beef and she sells it.

It is a mixed farm, about a third tillage, a third silage and a third grazing, and nearly everything the cattle eat is grown on it. Barley is harvested at the end of August and the grain is rolled on the farm as feed for the cattle. Silage is cut three times a year: grass first, then grass with whole crop peas and barley, then a last cut of grass. The only feed bought in is a nut from the mill down the road, for vitamins, and the farm sells grain back to that same mill.

The grazing is run on a tight rotation. Each field is split into three, the cattle graze three days in each part, and there are seven fields to a round, so no piece of ground sees them again for twenty one days. When the barley comes off, turnips go in, and kale is sown at the end of August. Over the winter the cattle strip graze them a metre a day behind an electric wire, working across the fields towards the house. Another cover crop holds the soil over the winter, fixes nitrogen, and whatever is not eaten by March is mulched back in.

Rathphelan is not an organic farm. Some fertiliser is used because the land is so boggy, the same bog the family once cut turf on, and it will not grow enough without help. Slurry and dung go back on the fields, and the reseeding, about a tenth of the farm each year, is going in with white clover, and red clover in the silage ground, so that each year it needs a little less fertiliser and assistance. A five acre field is sown with bird seed every May and left alone, something his father has done for ten years, and it has turned into a sanctuary for birds, with hawks and kestrels hunting over it.

The herd is Limousin and Charolais, around a hundred on the grass in summer and closer to two hundred through the winter, bought in from the same ten or so farmers they have dealt with for years. The next step is to breed their own: thirty Hereford heifers this November, in calf by January, with the first calves next autumn. The beef boxes are how the herd reaches people directly. Their beef is available to the community by the box, or as a quarter, half or whole animal, cut and labelled for the freezer, with next day delivery for anyone further afield.

The farm keeps its old machines running. There is a 1970s harvester that Liam and his father argue about selling every year, and never do. They have a beautiful selection of old tractors, John Deeres nearly all of them, and each has its own job: one for the bedding, one on narrow wheels for feeding and spraying in winter, one kept just for sowing potatoes, and one that runs the power washer. The only one that is not a John Deere is a 1976 tractor a neighbour left to his father in his will. There are very few wires on any of them, so when something breaks it is fixed in the yard with a set of spanners and a welder rather than sent to a dealer, and on a hot summer's day there is no better seat on the farm than the old tractor with no cab. Two old Volvos, bought for scrap, were rebuilt by his father and his uncle and both run perfectly.

products.name: Grass and clover
products.note: Grazed on a twenty one day rotation, each field split in three. Reseeded a tenth at a time, with more clover each year.

products.name: Silage
products.note: Three cuts off their own ground: grass, then grass with whole crop peas and barley, then grass again. Mixed on the farm and fed through the winter.

products.name: Home rolled barley
products.note: Grown here, harvested in late August and rolled in the yard on a roller they built themselves. Added as the cattle come in for finishing.

products.name: Kale
products.note: Sown after the barley and strip grazed a metre a day, or brought into the yard and mixed with the silage.

products.name: Turnips
products.note: Sown in early September straight after the barley, and grazed from the first of January across the field towards the house.

products.name: Nuts from the local mill
products.note: The one thing bought in, for the vitamins. The mill is down the road.
